Student can explain the difference between rational and irrational numbers.
Student can explain that the real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers.
Student can express a rational number in any format as a decimal.
Student can explain that rational numbers can be expressed in different forms, such as integers, fractions, and decimals.
Student can explain that a decimal expansion of a rational number can end in a repeating decimal.
Student can convert a decimal expansion into a different form of a rational number, such as a fraction.
Student can determine square roots of numbers.
Student can estimate rational and  irrational numbers and plot them on a number line.
Student can order and compare rational and irrational numbers.
Student can identify and explain the Pythagorean Theorem
Student can prove the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.
Student can apply the Pythagorean Theorem to solve problems involving two-dimensional figures, such as determining the side length of a right triangle.
Student can apply the Pythagorean Theorem to solve problems involving three-dimensional figures.
Student can apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points on the coordinate plane.
Student can use properties/laws of integer exponents to evaluate expressions.
Student can use properties/laws of integer exponents to generate equivalent expressions.
Student can use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 (scientific notation) to estimate very large and very small numbers.
Student can perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation.
Student can represent proportional relationships with tables, equations, and graphs.
Student can interpret unit rate as the slope of a graph of a proportional relationship.
Student can compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways (such as tables, equations, and graphs).
Student can use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane.
Student can derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b.

Student can determine the rate of change and initial value of a linear relationship from a description of the relationship or from two (x, y) values, including reading these from a table or from a graph.
Student can write an equation in the form y = mx + b to model a linear relationship between two quantities using verbal, numerical, tabular, and graphical representations.
Student can use the equation of a linear model to solve problems involving interpreting  slope and intercept.
Student can explain that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output.
Student can explain that a graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs consisting of an input and the corresponding output.
Student can compare properties of functions written in different ways (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
Student can identify linear functions and interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function whose graph is a straight line.
Student can give examples of functions that are not linear, such as the function A = s².
Student can construct a function to model a linear relationship between two quantities and interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models.
Student can describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear).
Student can sketch a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been described verbally.
Student can write equations with variables on both sides of the equal sign.
Student can solve linear equations with variables on both sides of the equal sign using the distributive property to collect like terms.
Student can solve linear equations involving fractions and decimals, including fractional and decimal coefficients.
Student can determine if a linear equation has one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions.
Student can explain that solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables correspond to points of intersection of their graphs.
Student can solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically.
Student can estimate solutions to systems of two linear equations by graphing the equations.
Student can solve simple cases of systems of two linear equations and two variables by inspection.
Student can solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
Student can explain and verify experimentally properties of translations.
Student can explain and verify experimentally properties of reflections.
Student can explain and verify experimentally properties of rotations.
Student can represent a geometric transformations algebraically.
Student can explain that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations.
Student can, given two congruent figures, describe a sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations between them.
Student can explain and verify experimentally properties of dilations.
Student can describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.
Student can represent dilation algebraically.
Student can explain that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations.
Student can, given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the similarity between them.
Student can use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles.
Student can use informal arguments to establish facts about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal.
Student can use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles.
Student can determine the sums of interior angles of regular polygons by decomposing them into triangles.
Student knows the formulas for the volume of a cone and can apply it to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
Student knows the formulas for the volume of a cylinder and can apply it to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
Student knows the formulas for the volume of a sphere and can apply it to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
Student can construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities.
Student can describe patterns in a scatter plot, such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.
Student understands that straight lines are widely used to model relationships between two quantitative variables.
Student can suggest a linear association, informally fit a straight line, and informally assess the model fit by judging the closeness of the data points to the line on a scatter plot.
Student can use the equation of a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
Student can make predictions and extrapolations based on trend lines.
Student understands that patterns of association in bivariate categorical data can be determined by displaying frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table.
Student can construct and interpret a two-way table summarizing data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects.
Student can use relative frequencies calculated for rows or columns of a two-way table to describe possible association between the two variables.
Probability
Student can solve real-world problems involving probabilities related to single or repeated experiments, including making predictions based on theoretical probability..
Grade 7
Modeling Addition and Subtraction of Rational Numbers (Number System)
Student can represent addition and subtraction on a number line.
Student can describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.
Student understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative.
Student can show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses).
Student can interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.
Student understands subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q).
Student can show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference.
Modeling Multiplication and Division of Rational Numbers (Number System)
Student can represent multiplication and division on a number line.
Student can explain that multiplication of rational numbers continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property.
Student can explain and apply the rules of multiplying signed (positive and negative) numbers.
Student can interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.
Student understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero.
Student understands that every quotient of integers (with a non-zero divisor) is a rational number.
Rational Numbers - Operations
Student can convert a rational number to a decimal using long division.
Student can explain that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.
Student can apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.
Student can apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.
Student can solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.
Rates
Student can compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.
Student understands and can apply unit rates in real-world contexts.
Rates and Proportionality

Student can determine whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Student can identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.
Student can represent proportional relationships with equations.
Student can graph proportional relationships.

Student can analyze graphs representing proportional relationships, including explaining what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.
Student can use proportional relationships to solve multi-step ratio problems.
Proportions and Percents
Student can determine percent increases or decreases.
Student can express rate of change as a percent.
Student can rewrite expressions in different forms to express rate of change as a percent increase or decrease.
Student can apply percents to find sales tax, tips, total cost, simple interest and other values in real-world contexts.
Expressions and Equations
Student can apply the Laws of Exponents to evaluate numerical expressions and generate equivalent numerical expressions.
Student can apply properties of operations to add and subtract linear expressions with rational coefficients.
Student can apply properties of operations to factor and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.
Student can explain how rewriting an expression in different forms in the context of a problem can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in the problem are related.
Student can write and solve one-step equations.
Student can construct one-step and two-step equations that model real-world or mathematical problems using variables to represent quantities..
Student can write and solve two-step equations.

Student can fluently solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers, including comparing algebraic with arithmetic solutions and identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.

Student can solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically, applying properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form, converting between forms as appropriate, and assessing the reasonableness of results using mental computation and estimation strategies.
Inequalities
Student can model and write one-step and two-step inequalities.
Student can solve one-step inequalities.
Student can solve two-step inequalities.
Student can solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers.
Student can graph the solution set of an inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
Modeling Geometric Figures
Student can explain scale drawings in the context of similar shapes.
Student can reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale.
Student can solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing.
Student can explain angle relationships, including facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles.
Student can construct triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
Student can use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.
Circumference, Area, and Volume
Student knows the formula for the circumference of a circle and use the circumference formula to solve problems.
Student knows the formula for the area of a circle and use the area formula to solve problems.
Student can give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.
Student can determine the area of composite two-dimensional figures.
Student can determine the surface area of prisms and right circular cylinders using nets.
Student can determine the volume of prisms and right circular cylinders.
Student can determine the surface area and volume of composite solids.
Random Sampling and Populations
Student can explain that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population.
Student can explain that generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population.
Student can explain that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
Student can use data from a random sample, represented in a table or dot or box plot, to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest.
Student can generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
Student can use proportional relationships to make predictions about a population.
Analyzing and Comparing Data
Student can analyze data represented in dot plots and box plots.
Student can represent proportional data in a circle graph.
Student can informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities.
Student can measure the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
Student can use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
Experimental Probability
Student can explain that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring and that larger numbers indicate greater likelihood.
Student can approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency,
Student can calculate experimental probability.
Student can predict approximate relative frequency given the probability of a chance event.
Theoretical Probability
Student can develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
Grade 6
Integers
Student can identify integers as the set of all positive and negative numbers without a fractional component and zero.
Student can explain that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values.
Student can use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation.
Student can compare and order integers.
Student can explain that the absolute value of a number is its distance from 0 on the number line.
Student can interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in real-world situations.
Student can determine the absolute value of an integer.
Rational Numbers
Student can classify rational numbers, including the identifying the relationship between natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, and rational numbers.
Student can represent division as a fraction.
Student can locate and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.
Student can identify opposites and absolute value of rational numbers.
Student can compare and order positive and negative rational numbers, including fractions, decimals and percent.
Student can locate and graph pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane, including numbers given in different forms (decimals, fractions, percentages).
Student can solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
Student can use coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.
Student can distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
Adding and Subtracting Integers
Student can model addition and subtraction of integers, including positive and negative numbers.
Student can add and subtract integers on a number line.
Student can subtract integers by adding the additive inverse.
Student can apply addition and subtraction of integers to solve real-world problems.
Multiplying and Dividing Integers
Student can model multiplying and dividing with integers.
Student can multiply integers with procedural fluency.
Student can model multiplication and division of integers on a number line.
Student can divide integers with procedural fluency.
Factors and Multiples
Student can explain factors, multiples, common factors, common multiplies, greatest common factor and least common multiple.
Student can find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100.
Student can find the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12.
Student can use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1-100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
Operations with Fractions
Student can apply greatest common factors (GCF) and least common multiples (LCM) to fraction operations.
Student can multiply and divide unit fractions and whole numbers.
Student can model fraction division as multiplying the dividend by the reciprocal of the divisor.
Student can model division of mixed numbers.
Student can divide mixed numbers with procedural fluency.
Student can solve multi-step problems involving fractions and mixed numbers.
Student can divide fractions with procedural fluency.
Representing Ratios and Rates
Student can explain the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.
Student can explain the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
Student can explain the concept of equivalent ratios.
Student can represent ratios using models.
Student can identify Pi as the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter.
Student can use ratio and rates to solve problems.
Applying Ratios and Rates
Student can make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole number measurements and find missing values in the tables.
Student can use tables to compare ratios.
Student can plot pairs of values in a table of equivalent ratios on the coordinate plane.
Student can use equivalent ratios to solve problems.
Student can solve unit rate problems, including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
Student can use a model to convert units.
Student can convert units using proportions and unit rates.
Student can use ratios and proportions to convert between measurement systems.
Percent
Student can model percent using a grid.
Student can explain the relationship between percents and fractions.
Student can write percents as fractions and decimals.
Student can solve real-world problems involving percents.
Equivalent Numerical Expressions
Generating Equivalent Algebraic Expressions
Equations and Relationships
Relationships in Two Variables
Student can write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.
Student can find factors and prime factorization of a number in the context of writing and evaluating numerical expressions.
Student can use order of operations to simplify numerical expressions.
Student can write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.
Student can identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms, including sum, term, product, factor, quotient, and coefficient.
Student can view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.
Student can evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables.

Student can perform arithmetic operations with algebraic expressions, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
Student can evaluate expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems.
Student can apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
Student can identify when two expressions are equivalent (i.e., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them).
Student can model equivalent expressions.
Student can explain that solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true?
Student can use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.
Student can use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem.
Student can explain that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
Student can use addition and subtraction to solve equations.
Student can use multiplication and division to solve equations.
Student can solve equations that represent geometric concepts.
Student can use inequalities to describe quantities.
Student can write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem.
Student can graph the solution to an inequality.
Student can identify that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.
Student can use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another.
Student can write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable.
Student can identify dependent and independent variables from tables and graphs.
Student can write equations to represent a real-world relationship.
Student can represent algebraic relationships in tables and graphs
Student can write equations from tables.
Student can use tables and equations to solve problems.
Relationships in Geometry
Student can find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes.
Student can solve real-world and mathematical problem involving the area of polygons and composite figures.
Student can draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices.
Student can use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.
Student can use techniques involving polygons on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
Solid Figures

Student can find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism.
Student can apply the formulas V = l w h and V = b h to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
Student can represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures.
Student can apply techniques related to nets and surface area of three-dimensional figures in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
Statistical Variability
Student can explain that a statistical question is one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.
Student can explain that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.

Student can explain that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.
Displaying, Analyzing, and Summarizing Data
Student can display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
Student can summarize numerical data sets by reporting the number of observations.
Student can summarize numerical data sets by describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.
Student can determine quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), of a data set.
Student can describe any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which a data set was gathered.
Student can relate the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

Student can write, interpret, and evaluate algebraic expressions in a real-world context.
Student can determine if a value assigned to a variable makes an equation true or false.

Student can use the addition, subtraction, multiplication and division properties of equality along with the associative, commutative, and distributive properties to justify the steps to solve an equation in one variable.
Student can create and solve equations in one variable that represent real-world situations.
Student can explain how to graph inequalities, including the addition and subtraction properties of inequalities.
Student can use the properties of inequality to solve inequalities with a focus on the multiplication property of inequality.
Student can solve compound inequalities and identify the differences between "and" and "or" compound inequalities.
Student can rearrange formulas in order to solve equations for a specified variable.
Student can represent the solutions to equations on a graph and determine if the functions are discrete or continuous.
Student recognizes that opposite signs of numbers indicate locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line.
Student recognizes that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., –(–3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite.
Student can fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.
Student can apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.
Student can develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
Student can explain that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.
Student can represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams.
For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), student can identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.
Student can design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
Student can describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, such as plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.
Student can express how many times larger or smaller one number written in scientific notation is than another written in the same format.
Non-Proportional Relationships
Student can represent linear relationships with tables, equations, and graphs.
Student can use graphs to determine rate of change and initial value.
Student can derive the slope-intercept form of an equation.
Student can graph non-proportional relationships using slope and y-intercept.
Student can compare properties of two different functions represented in different ways (such as tables, equations, and graphs).
Student can use the associative, commutative, and distributive properties to justify the steps to solve an equation in one variable.

Student can write recursive and explicit formulas when given a table of values, find terms using the formulas they create, and discover the connections between arithmetic sequences and linear functions.
Student can graph a series of real-world situations and then interpret  the rate of change using the context.
Student can comprehend the slope-intercept form of linear equations through writing equations of real world situations.
Student can discover the slope-intercept form of linear equations through writing equations of real world situations.
Student can discover the solution to a system is the point of intersection of the two lines.

Student can write and solve systems of linear equations that represent real-world situations, including discovering that the solution to a system of linear equations is the point of intersection of the two lines representing the equations..
Student can discover that equivalent systems have the same solutions.
Student can create inequalities from real-world situations and graph them on a coordinate plane.
Student can solve systems using elimination by creating equivalent systems of equations.
Student can find solution sets to systems of linear inequalities by writing a system of linear inequalities, graphing the system, and finding various solution sets.
Student can write two linear variable equations for a line that is parallel or perpendicular to a given line and goes through a given point.
Student can represent real-world situations in function notation and solve these situations.
Student can write and solve functions to represent real-world situations.
Student can classify polynomials by number of terms and degree.
Student can identify the leading term and leading coefficient of a polynomial.
Student can apply the properties of exponents to rewrite and identify equivalent expressions.
Student can apply number properties (commutative, associative, distributive) to rewrite polynomials as equivalent expressions.
Student can add and subtract polynomials written in function notation.
Student can apply methods of binomial multiplication (namely area model) to find products of binomials and polynomials.
Student can multiply polynomials using both modeling techniques and the distributive property.
Student can use the closure property with polynomials and analyze polynomials that are closed under the same operations as integers.
Student can apply knowledge of composition of function operations to real-world situations.
Student can describe solutions and intercepts of functions, when functions are increasing and decreasing, and relative maximums and minimums.
Student can determine rate of change over a specified interval.
Student can analyze the horizontal and vertical transformations of any function.
Student can solve expressions using an area model.
Student can find the factors of a quadratic equation and use the zero product property to determine the solutions.
Student can factor by grouping and use the distributive property to solve expressions.
Student can explain the zero product property and how it is used to solve equations.
Student can factor and solve quadratic equations not in standard form and quadratic equations with coefficients of the quadratic term not equal to one.
Student can factor and solve special cases of quadratic equations, including perfect square trinomials and the difference of squares.
Student can write equations for a function given the x-intercept and another point on the graph of a quadratic function.
Student can solve quadratic equations by taking the square root.
Student can complete the square of a quadratic equation and use this equivalent form to solve the equation.
Student can derive the quadratic formula by completing the square.
Student can use the quadratic formula to find solutions to quadratic equations.
Student can analyze a real-world situation where the rate of change is not constant.
Student can explain the key features of quadratic functions.
Student can interpret key features revealed when writing quadratic functions in equivalent forms represent in a real-world context.
Student can explain the vertex form of a quadratic function and create equations from the graph of the function.
Student can use the discriminant to determine the nature of solutions of quadratics equations.
Student can graph quadratic functions using a table of values.
Student can find the vertex and the intercepts and use the axis of symmetry to graph quadratic functions.
Student can rewrite the function in vertex form to reveal the vertex.
Student can rewrite functions not in vertex form to reveal the vertex.
Student can apply transformations of quadratic functions including vertical shifts, reflections, and vertical stretching and compressing.
Student can apply transformations of quadratic functions, including horizontal shifts, stretching and compressing.
Student can find solutions to quadratic equations by graphing, reading tables, algebraically and successive approximations.
Student can perform operations with rational numbers to add, subtract, multiply, and divide numerical radicals.
Student can apply the properties of exponents to rewrite and identify equivalent expressions.
Student can analyze operations and write proofs with rational and irrational numbers.
Student can craft generalizations on the relationships between rational and irrational numbers.
Student can rewrite expressions with radicals and rational exponents.
Student can apply the definition of rational exponents and properties of exponents to add expressions with radicals and rational exponents.
Student can apply the definition of rational exponents and properties of exponents to find products and quotients of expressions with radicals and rational exponents.
Student can explain the connection between geometric sequences and exponential functions.
Student can represent exponential functions as graphs in the coordinate plane and ordered pairs in tables.
Student can write equations of exponential functions.
Student can explain connection between the y-intercept, the rate of growth or decay, and end behavior..
Student can determine when a real-life situation can be modeled by an exponential growth or decay as well as determine the growth or decay factor.
Student can explain vertical and horizontal translations and compressions of exponential functions.
Student can compare and contrast the key features of linear, quadratic, and exponential functions.
Student can determine which type of sequence represents given situations.
Student can explain why the domains of sequences are a set or a subset of integers.
Student can write and solve a recursive and/or explicit formula for a sequence that is not arithmetic or geometric.
Student can model functions in situations given in a verbal, tabular, or graphical representation.
Student can graph piecewise defined functions within real-world contexts.
Student can explain absolute value functions and how they are an example of a piecewise-defined function.
Student can explain square root, cube root, and cubic functions.
Student can find the zeros of higher degree polynomial equations.
Student can recognize graphs of polynomial functions by finding the zeros.
Student can analyze end behavior of graphs of polynomials and sketch the graph of polynomials.

Student can identify the zeros of a polynomial and its end behavior depending on its leading coefficient and degree, and use this information to sketch a graph of a polynomial function in factored form.
Student can recognize even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions.
Student can analyze systems of polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions, and find solutions using tables and a graph.
Student can explain introductory statistical concepts, including two types of data: numerical and categorical.
Student can create dot plots.
Student can create histograms by determining the number of groups and the range of values within groups for that histogram.
Student can calculate number summaries and use this information to construct box plots.
Student can explain three common measures of center: mean, median, and mode.
Student can explain the difference between normal and skewed distributions and which measures of center are most appropriate given particular situations.
Student can explain two common ways to measure spread: interquartile range and standard deviation.
Student can explain the Empirical Rule and how it is used to measure spread in a normal distribution.
Student can explain how the Empirical Rule is used to determine probabilities in a normal distribution.
Student can interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).
Student can explain two-way frequency (contingency) tables as a way to represent two categorical variables.
Student can explain the difference between marginal frequencies and joint frequencies.
Student can explain conditional relative frequencies and how they can be used to determine if there is a relationship between two categorical variables.
Student can classify and interpret scatter plots and find the line of best fit using graphing technology.
Student can explain residuals and residual plots and how they are used to determine whether a certain function is a good fit for a model.
Student can define the concept of correlation, the correlation coefficient, and know what "r" tells us about the type of linear relationship between two variables.
Student can differentiate between correlation and causation.
